questions: What is the problem with this plot?
What is going on with my soil?
Explain the situation
answer: You are on a broad, flat plot of dark, heavy clay. It cracks deeply when dry, water sits on top for about a day after rain, and the surface then sets hard like a brick. Almost nothing grows. The likely cause is clay damaged by sodium, which makes it fall apart in water and seal its pores. It could also be salty soil or plain squashed clay, so check first with simple tests before you treat it.

questions: Do I need a lab test?
Can I use a pH meter?
What tools do I need?
answer: No lab and no instruments are needed. Every check uses your eyes, your hands and household items such as a cup, a spoon and a dark plate. Amounts are given as a handful, a bucketful, a pace or a hand's depth. Household checks are clues, not proof.

questions: What is a handspan?
What is a square pace?
What does hand's depth mean?
How much is a handful?
answer: A handful is what one hand can hold. A bucketful is one ordinary household bucket. A square pace is a patch one long step wide and one long step deep. A handspan is the distance from thumb tip to little fingertip with your hand stretched out. A hand's depth is as deep as your hand is long, which is the top layer where roots and water are active. A forearm length is from elbow to wrist.

questions: Is clear water safe?
Can I taste the water to check it?
Does a clean plate mean the water is safe?
Does a clear plate mean the water is safe?
answer: Never taste unknown water. Clear water, or a plate with no visible residue, does not prove the water is safe to drink or good for crops. Do not drink from an unknown source. For crops, use the cleanest known water and start with a small test bed.

questions: What is sodic soil?
What does sodium do to soil?
What is a slick spot?
answer: Sodic soil has too much sodium attached to its clay. The clay particles then let go of each other and fall apart in water, which blocks the tiny pores that let water in. It is also called a slick spot or black alkali. The surface seals, water ponds and the ground sets hard.
ref: Nevada and Oklahoma State extension guides

questions: What is salty soil?
What does salt do to plants?
What is saline soil?
answer: Salty soil has dissolved salts that collect near the surface as water dries in hot weather. They often show as a white or grey crust or powder. Salt can burn leaves and stop seeds from sprouting. Salty soil often stays crumbly and easy to work when it is not too wet.

questions: What is compacted clay?
What is plain heavy clay?
answer: Plain compacted clay is fine clay packed tightly by repeated wetting and drying, walking on it, and a lack of plant material. It drains slowly and has a hard surface. A dry crumb usually holds together or softens slowly instead of turning the water cloudy quickly.

topic: What is gypsum and why use it?
questions: What is gypsum?
What can I use as a calcium-rich amendment?
Can I use eggshells instead of gypsum?
Can I use shells or plaster scraps?
answer: Gypsum is a calcium-rich mineral sold for farming. Calcium helps sodium-affected clay particles stick together again, so water can enter. Use only known clean agricultural gypsum, only when the crumb check suggests sodium trouble, and begin with a small test strip. Eggshells, shells, old plaster scraps or household waste are not a substitute. A handful per square pace is a trial amount, not a whole-field repair.

topic: What is compost and why add it?
questions: What is compost?
Why add organic matter?
What is organic matter?
answer: Compost or organic matter is well-rotted plant material or old manure. In clay it helps form stable crumbs, opens channels for air and water, feeds soil life and reduces crusting.

questions: What is mulch?
Why use mulch?
answer: Mulch is a layer of dry grass, straw, leaves or crop leftovers laid on the soil, about a finger to a hand thick and kept a little away from young stems. It cushions raindrops, stops crusting, holds moisture, cools the soil and feeds it as it rots.

questions: What is a raised bed?
How high should a raised bed be?
answer: A raised bed is a low mound of soil, about a handspan to a forearm high, with a walking path or drainage furrow beside it. It keeps crop roots above the wettest layer.

questions: What is a drainage furrow?
How deep should drainage furrows be?
answer: A drainage furrow is a shallow channel about a handspan deep between beds that carries extra surface water away. Lead it only to a safe outlet away from wells, streams, homes and neighbouring fields. If there is no safe outlet, do not flush the plot.

questions: Why does the soil crack?
Why are there deep cracks when it is dry?
answer: Heavy clay shrinks when it dries and swells when it gets wet, so deep cracks open in dry weather. This is typical of this kind of clay. Cracks can also carry water down fast through a test hole and give a false impression that the whole plot drains well.

topic: Why does water sit on top after rain?
questions: Why does water sit on top of this soil after rain?
Why is water ponding on my soil?
Why does water not soak in?
answer: The heavy clay has lost its crumb structure and may be falling apart because of sodium. Loose clay blocks the pores that let water move down, so water ponds instead of soaking in. Flat land makes it worse because the water has nowhere to run off.

topic: Why not just flush the soil with lots of water?
questions: Why should I not just flush the soil with lots of water?
Can I flush the field if there is no drainage outlet?
Should I leach the soil?
answer: The soil already seals and ponds, so extra water just runs off or leaves roots waterlogged. In sodic soil, flushing alone may not bring back water entry. Calcium helps, and any salts released still need a safe way out. Do not flush a large area without a safe outlet. If there is no outlet, keep to one small raised bed and never send runoff toward wells, streams, homes or neighbouring fields.

topic: Why are there almost no weeds?
questions: Why are there almost no weeds?
Why does nothing grow?
answer: Almost no weeds points to a serious growing problem such as a sealed surface, too much salt, or too much sodium. It does not tell you which one. Look at which plants, if any, survive nearby for clues.

questions: Why do seedlings fail?
Why will seeds not come up?
answer: A hard crust blocks young shoots from pushing through, and roots cannot enter the dense, airless clay. Mulch, gentle watering, raised beds and careful loosening of the crust around seedlings all help.

topic: Can I use ash, greywater or salty manure?
questions: Can I use ash on this soil?
Can I use greywater?
Can I use salty manure or salty water?
answer: No, not where salt may be building up. These add salts and can make sprouting and root growth worse. Use the cleanest known water and well-rotted compost. Ash is also not recommended as a pest treatment here.

topic: When should I get local advice?
questions: What if the checks disagree or different patches behave differently?
When should I ask for local help?
What if results are unclear?
answer: If your checks disagree, the water used was unclear, or different patches behave differently, do not treat the whole field. Keep each patch separate, repeat the crumb, white-film and drainage checks with the clearest water you have, keep covering the soil, and use one small test bed. Ask nearby farmers or an agricultural officer if you can.

questions: How do I check if the soil is heavy clay?
What is the ribbon test?
answer: Take a walnut-sized moist lump from below the crust. Squeeze it between thumb and finger and try to make a ribbon. A long, smooth, sticky ribbon means heavy clay. A gritty or sandy feel means less clay. This shows the soil type, not the reason it seals. Repeat in more than one part of the plot.

topic: Dry crumb check (falls apart in water?)
questions: How can I tell whether this is a sodium problem without equipment?
How do I check if my soil is sodic?
How do I know if my soil is sodic?
How do I do the crumb test?
What is the crumb in water test?
answer: Drop a small dry crumb of soil into a clear cup or bowl of still water and wait several minutes without stirring. If it quickly falls apart and the water turns cloudy or milky, sodium trouble is possible. If it softens, swells or holds together without clouding the water quickly, plain compaction is more likely. This is a clue, not proof. Use the clearest water you have, and repeat in different patches.

questions: How do I check for salt?
What is the plate test?
What does a white crust mean?
answer: Look at the surface after it dries, especially in low spots and along puddle edges. Also dry a spoonful of site water on a dark plate or cloth. A pale film suggests dissolved material may be present, which points to salty soil. It does not say what the material is. A clean plate does not prove the water is safe.

questions: How do I test drainage?
What is the drainage hole test?
How fast should water drain?
answer: Dig a hole about a forearm deep and about as wide as a boot. Fill it with water and watch how fast it drains. Water that stays for a long time suggests poor drainage or a sealed layer. Use this to compare with your earlier results, not as a pass or fail mark. Deep cracks can let water vanish quickly, so repeat in another nearby spot after the soil is wet.

questions: How do I know it is sealing?
What does the crust tell me?
answer: After rain, watch whether water ponds, how long the surface stays wet and whether a hard skin forms as it dries. Ponding plus a hard, brick-like crust confirms a sealing problem. Deep cracks when dry are normal for clay that shrinks and swells.

questions: What do weeds tell me?
What plants grow nearby?
answer: Almost no weeds means a serious growing problem. Look for any plants that survive nearby. Salt-tolerant or waterlogging-tolerant weeds can give clues. No weeds alone cannot tell you the cause.

questions: What if the crumb clouds the water quickly?
What does a cloudy crumb mean?
Is my soil sodic?
answer: If a dry crumb clouds clear water quickly, there is little or no white film, and the surface seals and ponds, sodium-affected clay is possible. Treat this as a clue. First improve surface cover and drainage. Then try known clean agricultural gypsum on one small comparison strip only. Do not claim the strip will repair the whole plot.

questions: What if there is a white crust but the crumb stays whole?
Is my soil salty?
answer: A pale crust on the soil or a film on a dark plate, without strong crumb falling apart, points to possible salt build-up. Avoid salty inputs and unknown water. Improve drainage first. Do not flush unless the water can leave through a safe outlet.

topic: Signs point to both salt and sodium
questions: What if I see a white film and the crumb clouds the water?
Can it be both salty and sodic?
answer: A pale film plus a crumb that clouds the water quickly suggests salts and sodium may both be involved. Keep notes for each patch, protect your water and drainage, and start with a small test area only. Do not leach the whole plot without a safe outlet.

topic: Signs point to plain compacted clay
questions: What if the crumb does not cloud the water and there is no white film?
What if the crumb stays whole and there is no white film?
The crumb holds together and there is no salt crust, what is it?
Is it just compacted clay?
answer: Sticky heavy clay with ponding and crusting, but no fast cloudy crumb and no white film, points to plain compacted clay. Focus on compost, mulch, raised beds and staying off the soil when it is wet. Do not add calcium or flush without a reason.

topic: When the signs are mixed or unclear
questions: What if the checks disagree?
What if different patches behave differently?
What if I cannot tell what is wrong?
answer: If checks conflict, the water was unclear, or patches differ, do not diagnose or treat the whole field. Repeat each check separately with the clearest water you have, use low-risk surface cover, and keep planting to one small test bed. Ask for local advice if you can.

topic: Check each part of the plot separately
questions: Is the whole plot the same?
Should I test more than one spot?
answer: Check the wettest hollow, a crusted patch and a better-drained area separately and keep their results separate. A flat field can hold more than one soil condition.

topic: Sodic, salty or plain clay at a glance
questions: How can I tell salty soil from sodium-affected clay?
What is the difference between sodic and salty soil?
How do I tell the three apart?
answer: A pale crust or film suggests salt. A crumb that quickly clouds clear water suggests sodium. Both can happen together. If you see neither, plain compacted clay is more likely. These household checks do not identify the material or confirm the diagnosis.

questions: How does sodic soil feel?
Why are my puddles milky?
What does sodic soil look like?
answer: Sodium-affected soil often feels slick, soapy or greasy when wet. Puddles on top can look milky or cloudy, and a brownish-black crust may form. These are extra clues to add to your crumb check.
ref: Oklahoma State, Colorado State and Queensland government guides

topic: Salt can hide a sodium problem
questions: Can salty soil also be sodic?
Why does my crumb stay whole in salty soil?
Can flushing make it worse?
answer: In very salty soil, the salts can hold clay together, so a crumb may not fall apart even when sodium is high. If you wash the salt out without adding calcium, the soil can turn sodic and seal. This is another reason not to flush the whole plot.
ref: Queensland government and Soil Science Society guides

topic: What you still need to find out
questions: What is missing?
What do I still need to check?
What information is missing?
answer: Find out: does a dry crumb fall apart in still water, does a white film form on the soil or a dark plate, how fast does a filled hole drain, how good is the water source (unknown unless clearly known), and do different patches behave differently.

questions: Can I use the nearby water?
How do I check the water quality?
What if there is no water source?
answer: Dry a spoonful of the water on a dark plate. A visible film is a clue that dissolved material may be present. No film does not prove the water is safe or good for crops. Never taste unknown water. Use the cleanest known source, and begin with a small crop test. If there is no visible water source, collect clean rainfall if you can and keep it covered.

questions: Where do I start?
How do I plan the repair?
answer: Walk the plot slowly after rain. Mark the wettest patches, the places where water stays longest, the higher spots and where runoff leaves. This shows where to make drainage paths and where to focus repair. Reason: it saves effort and avoids making things worse.

topic: Run the crumb and white-film checks
questions: What checks should I do first?
answer: Do the dry crumb check in still water and dry a spoonful of site water on a dark plate. Reason: these two checks help separate sodium-affected clay from salty soil and plain compacted clay before you choose a treatment.

questions: How much compost should I add?
How do I add compost?
What can I use as organic matter?
answer: Mix well-rotted compost, old manure, leaf mould or rotted plant leftovers into the top hand's depth of soil. Use about one to two bucketfuls per square pace where you have it, and do not dig it in deep. Repeat over seasons. Reason: it helps clay form stable crumbs, opens air and water channels, feeds soil life and reduces crusting.

topic: Try clean gypsum on a small test strip
questions: How much gypsum should I use?
When should I use gypsum?
Should I add calcium?
answer: Only if the crumb check shows the crumb falling apart, and only if you have known clean agricultural gypsum or a locally recognised clean calcium material. Spread a light handful per square pace on one small test strip and leave an untreated strip next to it to compare. Do not use eggshells, shells, plaster scraps or household waste. Reason: calcium helps sodium-affected clay particles bind. This is a trial amount, not a whole-field repair.

questions: What should I avoid if the soil is salty?
Should I add ash or manure?
answer: If a pale residue suggests salt, do not add ash, salty manure, greywater or unknown salty water. Use the cleanest known water. Do not call water safe just because it looks clear. Reason: adding salts makes sprouting and root growth worse.

questions: How deep should drainage furrows be?
Where should drainage water go?
answer: Make shallow channels about a handspan deep between beds. Lead the water only to a safe, contained outlet that will not reach a well, stream, home or neighbouring field. If there is no safe outlet, do not flush the plot. Reason: furrows carry surface water away without damaging the soil below.

topic: Build raised or broad planting beds
questions: How high should the beds be?
Should I use raised beds?
answer: Form low raised beds about a handspan to a forearm high, wide enough to work comfortably, with walking space or a furrow between them. Reason: raised beds keep crop roots above the wettest layer and reduce waterlogging.

questions: How thick should mulch be?
What can I use for mulch?
answer: After planting, or between crops, lay dry grass, straw, leaves or crop leftovers about a finger to a hand thick, a little away from young stems. Reason: mulch cushions raindrops, reduces crusting, holds moisture, evens out soil temperature and adds organic matter as it rots.

topic: Water gently and in small amounts
questions: How should I water this soil?
How often should I water?
How do I water without making a crust?
answer: Use a perforated container, a cup or a slow trickle at the base of the plants, in the morning or evening. Stop when the surface starts to shine or water moves between beds. Repeat small amounts rather than one heavy flooding. Reason: gentle watering avoids crust and runoff.

topic: Keep living roots in the soil
questions: How do I keep the repair going?
What should I plant between crops?
answer: After harvest, return stems, leaves and roots to the soil or compost them nearby. Grow a hardy cover crop or a deep-rooted plant between main crops. Reason: living roots make channels, add organic matter and help hold the repaired structure.

topic: Grow a green manure crop such as dhaincha
questions: What is green manure?
What is dhaincha?
Can I grow a crop to improve sodic soil?
answer: Where seed is available locally, grow a fast, hardy green manure such as dhaincha (sesbania). Cut it while it is still green, around flowering, and mix it into the top hand's depth of soil. Reason: it adds plant material, helps water enter, keeps moisture longer, and has been used with gypsum to repair sodic land in India. Test a small patch first.
ref: Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) studies

topic: Check whether the test strip worked
questions: How do I know if gypsum worked?
Does gypsum need repeating?
What does a good gypsum result look like?
answer: Compare the treated strip with the untreated one after rain or watering. Good signs are water soaking in faster, less ponding, less crust and better seedling sprouting. The effect can fade over time, so you may need to repeat it over seasons. Only extend treatment to more ground if the strip clearly does better.
ref: Western Australia agriculture department and UC extension guides

topic: Protect the surface from rain, feet and crust
questions: Can I walk on wet soil?
How do I break the crust?
Why does the surface seal?
answer: Raindrops break soil crumbs and seal the surface, so keep the soil covered with mulch or plants. Do not dig or walk on it while it is wet and sticky, wait until it crumbles rather than smears. To help seedlings through, loosen the crust very lightly around them with a small hand tool without disturbing roots.
ref: USDA soil quality sheet and Oklahoma State extension

topic: Do not rush or overdo it
questions: What should I not do?
What are common mistakes?
Can I fix it in one season?
answer: Do not treat every hard, crusted soil as salty. Do not promise a full repair in one season. Do not bury mulch or compost deep, keep it in the top hand's depth. Do not call a handful-per-pace trial a whole-field rate. Keep comparing your test strip across seasons.

topic: Never do these with water and amendments
questions: What must I never do?
What is unsafe to do?
answer: Never taste unknown water. Do not leach a large area without a safe drainage outlet. Do not send salty runoff toward wells, streams, homes or neighbouring fields. Do not apply calcium when your checks do not point to sodium. Do not use eggshells, shells, plaster scraps or household waste instead of clean gypsum.

topic: Ready sign: the test hole drains sooner
questions: When is the soil ready for planting?
How do I know the soil is ready?
What is the readiness gate?
answer: Start or expand planting only when a filled test hole drains sooner than it did before and does not stay ponded for a long time. Compare more than one patch, because deep cracks can mislead the check. These are comparisons with your own earlier results, not universal marks.

topic: Ready sign: no hard crust after watering
questions: How do I know the crust is improving?
answer: A light watering should no longer leave a hard crust after it dries.

topic: Ready sign: the crumb check improves
questions: How do I know the sodium problem is improving?
answer: Where sodium trouble was suspected, the crumb should fall apart less quickly and cloud the water less than before. Treat this as a clue, not proof.

topic: Ready sign: no strong new salt film
questions: How do I know the salt is not getting worse?
answer: There should be no strong new visible salt film. A clean-looking plate does not certify water safety or suitability for crops.

topic: Ready sign: the test crop survives
questions: How do I test with a crop first?
answer: A small patch of a locally adapted crop should sprout and survive its first waterings before you expand.

topic: Ready sign: excess water has a safe outlet
questions: Where should extra water go?
answer: Any extra water must have a safe way out that will not reach wells, streams, homes or neighbouring fields.

topic: If the soil is not ready yet
questions: What if the soil is not ready?
What should I do next if nothing improves?
answer: Keep working on the test bed, keep the soil covered, improve safe surface drainage, and repeat the checks in separate patches. If results stay unclear, avoid whole-field amendments or flushing and ask for local agricultural advice if you can.

topic: Compare against your own first result
questions: How do I track progress?
How do I know it is getting better?
answer: Note what each check looked like on day one for each patch, such as how cloudy the crumb water was, how long the hole stayed full and how hard the crust was. Repeat the same checks after each treatment and each season, and compare patch by patch.

questions: Which crops should I try first?
Which crops can grow here?
Are all listed crops tolerant of waterlogging and sodicity?
answer: Tolerance to wet soil, to heat and drought, to salt, and to sodium are different traits, and a crop may have only one of them. Put wet-soil crops in moist zones with managed water and dryland crops on better-drained raised beds. Choose local varieties and test a small patch before you scale up.

questions: Can I grow taro?
What crop suits the wet patches?
answer: Where: moist patches that drain slowly. Why: it copes with wetter soil better than many dryland crops. How: plant on a raised bed or broad ridge and test a small patch first. Limit: liking wet soil does not mean it handles salt or sodium, so choose a local variety.

questions: What other crops tolerate wet soil?
answer: Where: seasonally wet patches where the crop is already grown locally. Why: local wetland crops may suit repeated wetness better than dryland crops. How: choose varieties known in your area and keep a small test patch. Limit: do not assume salt or sodium tolerance from waterlogging tolerance.

questions: Can I grow rice here?
Is rice good for sodic soil?
answer: Where: only where water is reliable and the field can be managed without unsafe runoff. Why: it handles saturated soil better than most dryland crops, and in India rice grown on sodic land has been shown to help repair it. How: use it only if your climate, seed and water supply fit. It is not the default for a dry plateau. Limit: it does not remove the need to manage salt and drainage.

questions: Can I grow sorghum?
Which crop handles heat and irregular rain?
answer: Where: better-drained raised beds or ridges once the worst ponding has eased. Why: it suits hot weather and irregular water better than delicate crops. How: use locally adapted seed and a small test patch. Limit: heat and drought tolerance is not the same as tolerance to long waterlogging, salt or sodium.

questions: Can I grow millet?
Which crop suits dry poor soil?
answer: Where: better-drained raised beds or ridges where water is scarce. Why: it suits hot, dry conditions and fairly poor soil. How: sow once the surface is no longer sealing so badly, and mulch after it is up. Limit: keep it out of the wettest hollows and do not assume it tolerates salty soil.

questions: Can I grow pigeon pea?
Which crop has deep roots?
answer: Where: better-drained areas or plot edges, not waterlogged hollows. Why: a longer-season crop with deep roots once established. How: use as a locally familiar longer-season crop or intercrop. Limit: deep roots alone will not repair a sealed sodic layer.

questions: Can I grow beans?
Which legume suits this soil?
answer: Where: raised beds or ridges with better drainage. Why: it gives food and leftover plant material for the soil where local varieties establish well. How: do not sow into a sealed crust, and test a small patch first. Limit: tolerance to waterlogging and salt differs between crops and varieties.

questions: Can I grow sunflower?
Is there an oilseed crop for this soil?
answer: Where: better-drained ground after water entry improves. Why: a suitable local oilseed adds variety to the rotation and keeps roots in the soil. How: use only where seed and local experience support it. Limit: do not claim deep roots alone will break a hard or sodic layer.

questions: Can I grow pumpkin?
Which crop covers bare soil?
answer: Where: raised mounds in better-drained areas. Why: spreading leaves cover bare soil and soften raindrop impact. How: plant in a small mound with compost and train the vines over bare ground. Limit: avoid low hollows with long ponding, and use a locally adapted variety.

questions: What can protect the plot edges?
Can I plant grass?
answer: Where: plot edges and stable drainage lines, not the crop beds. Why: dense roots protect bare soil and slow surface runoff. How: use only a locally suitable grass that will not block drainage. Limit: this protects soil and is not necessarily a food crop.

questions: Can I grow leafy greens?
Which crop is fastest?
answer: Where: a well-mulched raised bed with compost. Why: a quick crop that shows early whether your repair is working. How: sow lightly, keep the soil covered and water gently. Limit: tender greens are easily hurt by crust, standing water or salty water, so use the cleanest known water.

questions: Is there a crop that repairs the soil?
Can I grow dhaincha?
answer: Where: bare beds before the main crop. Why: a fast, hardy, nitrogen-fixing plant used in India to rebuild sodic and salty land. How: grow it first, cut it while green, mix it into the top hand's depth, then plant your main crop. Limit: it is for soil repair, not food. Use local seed and test a small patch.

questions: How long will repair take?
How long until the soil is fixed?
Will it be fixed this season?
answer: You may see some improvement after one season of compost, mulch, careful watering and root growth. Full repair usually takes more than one season. Plan at least one full season of repair before expecting the whole plot to do well, and start with a small test bed.

questions: How long do leafy greens take?
answer: Leafy greens usually mature in about 3-6 weeks. Allow about 4-10 weeks once you include a buffer for slow soil repair.

topic: Time to harvest: cowpea or hardy bean
questions: How long do cowpea or beans take?
answer: Cowpea or hardy bean usually matures in about 8-12 weeks. Allow about 10-18 weeks with the repair buffer.

questions: How long does pearl millet take?
answer: Pearl millet usually matures in about 10-14 weeks. Allow about 12-20 weeks with the repair buffer.

questions: How long does sorghum take?
answer: Sorghum usually matures in about 14-20 weeks. Allow about 16-28 weeks with the repair buffer.

topic: Time to harvest: pumpkin or gourd
questions: How long does pumpkin take?
answer: Pumpkin or gourd usually matures in about 12-18 weeks. Allow about 14-26 weeks with the repair buffer.

questions: How long does taro take?
answer: Taro usually matures in about 6-10 months. Allow about 7-14 months with the repair buffer.

questions: How long does pigeon pea take?
answer: Pigeon pea usually matures in about 4-8 months. Allow about 5-12 months with the repair buffer.

questions: How accurate are the timings?
Are these timings guaranteed?
answer: These timings are planning ranges. They change with the local variety, the season, the water and how well the crop establishes. They describe crop timing only. They are not a promise of soil repair or yield.

questions: What bed type should I use?
Where do I plant what?
answer: Use raised beds or broad ridges in the better-draining areas, mounds for spreading vines, and keep the wettest patches for water-tolerant crops only.

questions: How high should I raise the beds?
answer: Raise beds about a handspan to a forearm high. Go higher where water stays longer after rain.

questions: Where do furrows go?
answer: Make shallow furrows about a handspan deep between beds, leading only to a safe outlet away from wells, streams, homes and neighbouring fields. If there is no safe outlet, do not flush the plot.

questions: What should I add to the bed?
How much compost per bed?
answer: Mix about one to two bucketfuls of well-rotted compost or old manure per square pace into the top hand's depth. If the crumb check showed sodium trouble, use a light handful of known clean agricultural gypsum on a small comparison strip only. This is not a whole-field amount.

questions: How do I sow seeds here?
How many seeds per hole?
How deep should I sow?
answer: Sow when the surface has dried enough to crumble rather than smear. Make shallow holes or furrows only as deep as the seed needs. Put two or three seeds in each hole and thin later to the strongest. Cover seeds lightly with fine soil or compost, not heavy clay. After seedlings come up, add a thin mulch kept away from the stems.

questions: How should I water the new seedlings?
How do I avoid ponding and crusting?
answer: Water gently at the base of the plants with a perforated container or slow trickle. Give small amounts often rather than flooding. Stop when the surface starts to shine or water moves toward the furrows. After each watering, check for ponding, crusting and wilting seedlings.

topic: Water is limited: use one test bed
questions: What if I have little water?
What if rain is my only water?
answer: If water is limited, put your effort into one well-mulched test bed rather than the whole plot. If rain is your only source, collect clean rainfall where you can and keep it covered so it stays clean.

topic: No safe outlet for extra water
questions: What if there is nowhere for the water to go?
answer: If there is no safe outlet, do not flush the plot. Build a small raised test bed instead, and do not send runoff toward wells, streams, homes or neighbouring fields.

topic: Water at the right time of day
questions: When should I water?
What time of day is best to water?
answer: Water in the early morning or evening where you can, so less water is lost to the sun.

questions: What should I do before sowing?
answer: Confirm the soil type with the crumb, plate, ribbon and drainage-hole checks. Prepare raised beds and furrows. Add compost or old manure to the top hand's depth. Use a calcium material only if the crumb check shows the crumb falling apart. Watch for water still ponding for more than about a day and for a surface that smears when pressed.

topic: Care at germination and seedling stage
questions: How do I care for seedlings?
What do I do when seedlings come up?
answer: Water gently, and only when the top soil starts to dry. Add a thin mulch once seedlings are up. Carefully lift the crust around seedlings without disturbing roots. Thin to the strongest seedling once true leaves appear. Watch for seedlings trapped under crust, yellowing from waterlogging, or wilting between waterings.

questions: How do I care for growing plants?
answer: Keep the mulch topped up and the furrows open. Feed lightly with well-rotted compost or manure and avoid fresh or visibly salty material. Check moisture and drainage before adding more feed if plants look pale or slow. Stay off wet beds. Watch for yellow lower leaves after watering, standing water, hard crust or stunted growth.

questions: How do I care for flowering plants?
answer: Keep moisture steady with small, gentle waterings and mulch. Avoid sudden flooding or long dry spells. Support tall or fruiting plants if needed, and weed carefully so weeds do not steal water. Watch for flower or fruit drop after waterlogging, wilting, or leaf burn, which can point to salty water or salt build-up.

questions: What fertilizer should I use?
How do I feed plants in clay?
answer: Use small amounts of well-rotted compost or old manure. Avoid fresh manure and anything visibly salty. If plants look pale or slow, first check moisture and drainage before adding more. Do not overfeed.

questions: What should I check after watering?
How do I know I watered too much?
answer: After each watering, look for three things. Is water ponding or shining on the surface? Is a crust starting to form? Are seedlings wilting? If you see ponding or crust, water less next time and loosen the crust gently.

topic: Disease watch in poorly drained soil
questions: What diseases should I watch for?
How do I prevent root rot?
answer: Do not overcrowd plants so air can move. Remove diseased leaves and plant debris, and keep leaves and fruit off wet soil. Watch for damping-off, root rot, leaf disease, pests and signs of water stress.

questions: What can I use for pests?
Can I use neem?
Can I use ash for pests?
answer: If pests appear, use a locally approved neem-based or other plant-based spray as local guidance says, and test it on a few leaves first. Do not spray open flowers, and keep sprays out of wells, streams and drainage water. Do not use ash as a pest treatment here.

topic: Yellow leaves can have several causes
questions: Why are my leaves turning yellow?
Is yellowing a nutrient problem?
answer: Yellowing can come from wet roots or salt stress as well as a lack of nutrients. Do not decide it is a nutrient shortage from colour alone. First check drainage, crust and water quality.

questions: How do I know grains are ripe?
answer: Seed heads turn from green to dry, tan or brown, and the seeds feel hard and resist fingernail pressure.

questions: How do I know beans are ripe?
answer: Pods dry out, turn pale or brown and rattle slightly when shaken.

questions: How do I know roots are ready?
answer: Leaves yellow and die back. Gently uncover the shoulder of the root to check its size before lifting.

questions: How do I know a pumpkin is ripe?
answer: The skin hardens, the colour changes to the mature shade for the variety, and the stem begins to dry.

questions: How do I harvest leafy greens?
answer: Pick the outer leaves when they are large enough and let the centre keep growing.

questions: How do I harvest?
When is the best time to harvest?
How do I dry the harvest?
answer: Harvest when the soil is moist but not sticky, and not right after heavy rain. Cut grain heads or pods cleanly and dry them in an airy, shaded place before storing. Lift root crops gently with a hand tool or stick so they do not break in hard clay. Do not drag harvest containers across wet beds.

questions: What should I do after harvest?
Should I burn the stalks?
answer: Return stalks, leaves and roots to the soil or compost them nearby. Do not burn usable leftovers unless disease makes it necessary. Return healthy residues to the soil or compost them nearby, and keep the soil covered.

questions: How do I keep the soil improving?
What should I plant after harvest?
answer: Add compost or well-rotted manure again to the top hand's depth. Replant with a cover crop, hardy bean, deep-rooted crop or local grass so living roots stay in the ground. Keep the mulch and drainage furrows in place.

questions: How do I know the soil is improving?
What do I do next season?
answer: At the start of the next season, repeat the dry crumb and white-film checks in the same zones. See whether the structure is improving and the salt film is not growing. Expand only where the soil and your test crop have improved.
